acceptance_criteria.criterion: Registered handlers are invoked when both the request method and URL pattern match
A 404 JSON response is returned when no registered pattern matches the request path
A 405 JSON response is returned (with a correct Allow header) when the path matches but the HTTP method does not
Named path segment extraction (:param syntax) is correctly resolved and passed to the handler as a params object
Router is covered by unit tests for match, 404, and 405 scenarios

summary: Implemented Router class in src/server/router.ts and the full unit test suite in src/server/__tests__/router.test.ts. All 17 tests pass; existing requestUtils tests (25) are unaffected."

comments.note: router.ts is dependency-free and delegates all param extraction to extractParams() from requestUtils — no duplication. The 405 Allow header deduplication is handled via Array.includes() on a small array, which is fine for the expected number of registered methods per route.

Handler async errors are swallowed via void Promise.resolve().catch() to prevent unhandledRejection crashes; handlers are expected to write their own error responses, consistent with the minimal-dependency philosophy of the module.

metrics.test_coverage: All 5 AC paths and 17 router-specific tests pass

comments.note: The 405 response path (router.ts:102-107) uses inline res.writeHead/res.end rather than sendError/sendJson. As a result it does not set a Content-Length header, unlike 404 which goes through sendError→sendJson. Functionally correct and not a bug, but a cosmetic inconsistency worth noting for the code-review pass.

Async handler errors are intentionally swallowed via void Promise.resolve().catch(). This is by design (handlers own their error responses) and is safe — no unhandledRejection will leak. Consistent with project philosophy.

req.url and req.method undefined guards (?? '/' and ?? 'GET') are present and correct. Method is uppercased before matching so lowercase HTTP methods (e.g. 'get') are normalised — covered by a dedicated test.

No test exercises a route registered after handle() is first called (dynamic route registration at runtime). Not part of the spec, but worth mentioning if the Router is ever extended to support runtime registration.

summary: WP-003 code review PASS. router.ts is clean, well-typed, and dependency-free beyond its deliberate reuse of extractParams/sendError from requestUtils. Logic is correct and readable; test suite is comprehensive (17 tests, all AC paths covered). One low-priority improvement noted: the 405 path uses inline res.writeHead/res.end instead of sendError, omitting Content-Length. This is a cosmetic inconsistency with the 404 path and does not affect correctness. No blocking issues.

comments.note: router.ts:102-106 — the 405 response writes headers with inline res.writeHead/res.end, bypassing sendError→sendJson. This means Content-Length is not set on 405 responses, whereas 404 goes through sendJson and always sets Content-Length. Functionally fine for HTTP/1.1 chunked responses, but inconsistent with the rest of the module's response handling style. Consider routing 405 through sendError in a future pass for uniform behaviour.
void Promise.resolve(entry.handler(...)).catch(() => {}) at router.ts:92-95 is the correct pattern for async-safe fire-and-forget. Well commented. No issue.

The private register() helper is clean and keeps the four HTTP verb methods DRY. Returning `this` enables fluent chaining — a nice touch, although not exercised in tests. Consider adding a chaining test in a future iteration for completeness.

No public method to register arbitrary HTTP verbs (e.g. PATCH, HEAD, OPTIONS). This is in-scope for the current WP and fine, but worth a note if the server ever needs to handle PATCH or HEAD requests.
No issues found — code is clean, consistent, and well-structured overall.
